BC teachers say public education is being overlooked in the provincial election campaign

=== MULTI-SOURCE TOPIC CLUSTER: BC teachers say public education is being overlooked in the provincial election campaign ===

[Source 1 — pressprogress.ca] (URL: https://pressprogress.ca/bc-teachers-say-public-education-is-being-overlooked-in-the-provincial-election-campaign/):
Stated Claim / Post Context:
BC teachers say public education is being overlooked in the provincial election campaign

Rank-and-file teachers want political parties to pledge to “redirect public funding to public schools.”

Actual Article Body:
Charles Hays Secondary School, Prince Rupert, BC (Wikimedia Commons)

Rank-and-file teachers want political parties to pledge to “redirect public funding to public schools.”

A group of rank-and-file teachers is warning that public education has been sorely missing from BC’s provincial election.

RECESS, the teacher-led campaign, is asking candidates to pledge to “support the redirection of public funding to public schools,” as provincial funding for private schools continues to increase.

Tara Ehrcke, a member of RECESS, said the group is working with the Coalition for Public Education to bring the issue of public education back into the conversation during the campaign.

“I’ve been a teacher for 20 years. I teach high school math in Greater Victoria, and it has been disappointing, I’d say, that there hasn’t been more discussion around education and education funding and schools,” Ehrcke told PressProgress.

Ehrcke said that BC currently has a “two-tiered system” in education, where public funding is being diverted away from the public school system into the private sector.

Two-tiered system

According to the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives, between the 1999-2000 and 2025-26 school years, spending on public schools in BC increased by 32%, while funding for private schools increased by 50%.

Annual funding increases for private schools over the last decade have also drastically outpaced increases for public schools.

“What we have is actually a subsidized two-tier system, where the people who are using private schools get public subsidies for it,” Ehrcke said. “What we’ve also seen in those years is the percentage of people sending their kids to private schools has increased.”

Ehrcke added that per-student funding follows students where they go. When parents who can afford it send their kids to private schools, it creates a funding shortfall in the public system.

“When you have 50% per student funding following kids to those private schools, and then you have kids moving from the public system to the private system, and that’s where that bigger increase comes from,” Ehrcke said. “Of course there’s only a limited number of people who are going to actually be able to afford that.”

According to the coalition, there was a $317 million dollar shortfall for inclusive education in public schools in the 2024/25 school year.

In some cases, private schools offer programming for children with learning challenges who aren’t well-served in the public school system. When their parents can afford private school and choose to send their children there, the funding follows, making it even harder for the public school system to establish those programs.

“It’s a terrible kind of cycle where you pull this funding out of the public system and then it becomes harder and harder for the public system to actually be providing those services,” Ehrcke explained.

She said that the lack of funding also contributes to persistent issues with buildings that don’t get fixed and an overall lack of teachers in the province.

“It’s more than an entire year’s education budget just to get our buildings up to the standard they ought to be. And that’s because we’ve had these years and years of not enough money. Our facilities are in terrible shape province-wide,” Ehrcke said.

“We actually have a teacher shortage in British Columbia as well — if you go up to more remote parts of the province, there’s a lot of people teaching who are not actually qualified teachers because there’s no qualified teachers available to fill those jobs.”

Party pledges on education

While Ehrcke was clear that more investment in education is needed across the board, she shared her concerns around what could happen under a BC Conservative government.

“I’ve been teaching for 20 years and it was really, really difficult under the BC Liberals where every year there were different assaults on the education system one way or another,” Ehrcke said.

“Certainly we don’t see that kind of assault on public education under the NDP, but what we don’t see either is the really necessary investment.”

Ehrcke said that it is important for the parties to take the RECESS pledge to support public funds for public education, especially in an election that is expected to be close in key ridings in the Interior, Victoria and Surrey.

She shared that Sara Lopez, the BC NDP candidate in North Island, became the first BC NDP candidate to sign their pledge. The NDP has started or completed 250 major school capital projects since 2017.

Denice Bardua, the NDP candidate for Prince George-North Cariboo, has said that attracting and retaining teachers in northern BC is important, given that rural and remote areas don’t receive enough resources. =

“Has the NDP responded in crisis situations like in Surrey or in Langford where schools were so overcrowded? Yes, they’ve built some schools, but is it anything near what is necessary? Absolutely not,” Ehrcke said, noting that counsellors and more staffing are still needed in many school districts.

Meanwhile, the BC Conservatives platform doesn’t include commitments to invest in education, instead focusing on “repealing SOGI 123,” which stands for ‘sexual orientation gender identity’ and is a set of resources regarding the 2SLBTQ+ community. The party also commits to “bringing back letter grades” from grades 4-9.

Additionally, the Conservatives promise to” bring back the singing of ‘O Canada’ at the beginning of the school day and proudly fly our Canadian and BC flags at every school.”

Ehrcke said that the BC Greens have provided the most fulsome plan for public education, including closing the ‘inclusion gap’, increasing the number of counsellors in schools, expanding support for SOGI, and a climate resilience plan to address the impact of climate change on classrooms.

According to the BC Teacher’s Federation, school districts spend more on inclusive education every year than they receive in funding from the Ministry of Education and Childcare.

“We can feel very righteous sometimes in Canada and think that our social services are not like what we see down south. But in the education context, it is essentially a voucher system: That 50% per-student funding follows your child to a private or independent school,” Ehrcke said.

Ehrcke said the amount of public money going to private schools would be enough to close the inclusion gap.

“It doesn’t require any new taxes or increasing the deficit. It’s simply redirecting the public funding into public schools,” said Ehrcke.

The BC NDP and BC Conservatives did not respond to questions from PressProgress regarding their plan for public education prior to publication.

Mayor Brandon Johnson, center, displays a signed executive order establishing the Chicago Market City Implementation Steering Committee alongside Ald. Chris Taliaferro (29th). Johnson is joined by Greater Chicago Food Depository CEO Kate Maehr (left); Anton Seals Jr., lead steward of Grow Greater Englewood; and Cinnamon Sanchez, market manager of the Austin Town Hall City Market.

Victor Hilitski/For the Sun-Times

Share

Mayor Brandon Johnson wants to increase food access by creating a community-based “market city” framework, with priority attention given to the historically underserved South and West sides.

Johnson’s new plan, called the Market City Action Plan, was announced Thursday and would further his 2025 idea to establish a public market. It calls for creating administrative infrastructure to provide resources for food entrepreneurs, supporting existing farmers markets and building a network of year-round indoor public markets.

He also signed an executive order to establish a steering committee that would bring together city departments and community members to implement the plan. Johnson appointed Aaliayah Romer as manager of food equity to head the initiative.

“Our Market City strategy is about building a food system that responds to what communities need while creating more opportunities for local entrepreneurs to grow and succeed,” Johnson said in a news release. “This executive order moves that vision into action so we can deliver lasting solutions shaped by the needs of our neighborhoods.”

Johnson first floated the idea of expanding food access in 2023 when he proposed a city-owned grocery store. Following a feasibility study on the idea, he pivoted to opening public markets.

“After a very thoughtful and a more thorough engagement over the last several years, listening to people, we heard loud and clear that the entrepreneur spirit of Chicagoans wanted their efforts to be strengthened, and especially Chicago’s existing food ecosystem. So it was important that we’re building on the innovative work that’s already happening in our neighborhoods,” Johnson told the Chicago Sun-Times Thursday.

Residents on the South and West sides statistically have much lower access to grocery stores than other neighborhoods. A report released this year by the Greater Chicago Food Depository found 51% of South Side homes, 45% of West Side homes and 41% of Southwest Side homes are food insecure and don’t have consistent access to enough food.

Johnson’s announcement comes three months after the city-funded redevelopment deal with the operators of Save A Lot fell apart after the owner, Yellow Banana, closed its seven stores one year after opening.

Following the Save A Lot closures, the city announced in August that it would provide $450,000 in microgrants through its Neighborhood Market Grant Program to help support existing grocers and markets.

Johnson’s new plan was developed over the last year in collaboration with the Chicago Food Equity Council and the Greater Chicago Food Depository, as well as community stakeholders such as residents, entrepreneurs, farmers and market operators.

The mayor’s office said the next step will be to release a request for information to the public in the next month, with the goal of identifying potential sites and operators for a market.

Residents would likely see the first results of the plan through additional support to farmers markets during the 2027 season, said Ruby Ferguson, senior director of community engagement at the Greater Chicago Food Depository. The support could be financial or through marketing help.

Johnson said the city is still considering whether it will own or operate the public markets and that it may instead provide support.
